reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society clinical guidance
clinicalPearls: A 46,XX individual with a female phenotype, normal internal mullerian structures, but bilateral streak gonads that fail to produce oestrogen
Typically presents with primary amenorrhoea and absent or arrested puberty in a girl of normal stature, without the somatic stigmata of Turner syndrome
Biochemistry shows hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with high gonadotropins and low oestradiol

Often inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with variants in genes such as FSHR and other ovarian-determining and DNA-repair genes; some cases form part of syndromes (for example Perrault syndrome with sensorineural deafness)
The uterus is present and normal, so pregnancy is achievable through oocyte donation after adequate hormonal preparation
Unlike dysgenesis involving a Y chromosome, there is no gonadoblastoma risk, so prophylactic gonadectomy is not indicated on tumour grounds
Management centres on oestrogen and progestogen replacement to induce puberty, maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone
reference.pathophysiology: In 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis the karyotype is normal female, but the ovaries fail to develop and are replaced by fibrous streak gonads, so oestrogen production is absent. This may follow biallelic defects in genes required for ovarian development or gonadotropin signalling (such as the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor) or occur within multisystem syndromes. The mullerian ducts, whose development does not depend on gonadal hormones, form a normal uterus and upper vagina, while the absence of oestrogen prevents pubertal maturation and drives compensatory elevation of gonadotropins. Because no Y-chromosome material is present, the streak gonads do not carry the germ cell tumour risk seen in Y-bearing dysgenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Turner syndrome and its mosaic forms
Premature ovarian insufficiency of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype confirming 46,XX and excluding a Y-bearing line
Serum follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and oestradiol demonstrating hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
Pelvic ultrasound or MRI confirming a uterus and streak gonads
Genetic testing including FSHR and syndromic genes where indicated
Audiometry to detect associated sensorineural hearing loss (Perrault syndrome)
Bone mineral density assessment given oestrogen deficiency
redFlags: Associated sensorineural deafness or neurological features suggesting a syndromic diagnosis
Severe osteoporosis or fragility fracture from untreated oestrogen deficiency
Delayed diagnosis with prolonged absence of pubertal development
Any evidence of a Y-chromosome line on karyotype, which would change tumour-risk management
reference.prognosis: With oestrogen and progestogen replacement, pubertal development and bone health can be established and maintained, and pregnancy is feasible through oocyte donation because the uterus is intact. The absence of a Y line means germ cell tumour risk is not a concern in this karyotype.
pitfalls: Attributing primary amenorrhoea to constitutional delay and missing hypergonadotropic hypogonadism
Recommending gonadectomy despite the absence of a Y chromosome and tumour risk
Confusing it with androgen insensitivity, in which the uterus is absent
Overlooking associated syndromic features such as deafness
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on disorders of sex development
